title: Bits, bytes & how computers work
summary: Begin with the physical and logical foundations: binary numbers, instructions, memory, storage, and the CPU.
html:
Begin with the physical and logical foundations: binary numbers, instructions, memory, storage, and the CPU.

How the pieces connect

From voltage to information

Digital circuits interpret ranges of electrical states as 0 and 1. A bit stores one binary choice. Eight bits form a byte and encode 256 distinct patterns. Meaning comes from an agreed representation: the same bits can be interpreted as an integer, a character, or part of a floating-point number.

A program is data plus instructions

A processor fetches instructions, decodes them, operates on registers, and reads or writes memory. Modern CPUs overlap work, predict branches, and cache recently used data. A thread is an instruction stream with its own execution state. Multiple cores can execute multiple streams; dependencies still limit what can happen simultaneously.

The storage hierarchy

Registers are small and close to arithmetic units. Caches retain likely-to-be-reused memory. RAM holds a running program’s working set. SSDs persist files but are much slower for fine-grained access. Moving a model from disk to RAM to GPU memory is real work, even if a framework hides the transfers.

Units that prevent expensive mistakes

A decimal GB is 10^9 bytes; a GiB is 2^30 bytes. Bandwidth is data per second; latency is time until a result arrives. Frequency counts clock cycles per second, not completed useful operations. Model parameter count measures stored learned values, not token capacity or reasoning ability.

Worked example

An 8-billion-parameter model with one 16-bit value per parameter needs 8×10^9×2 = 16 GB, or about 14.90 GiB, for weights alone. Runtime buffers and a KV cache consume additional memory. A 16 GB device is therefore not guaranteed to fit it.

What goes wrong

Confusing Gb with GB introduces an eightfold error. Assuming all installed memory is available ignores the operating system, other processes, and runtime allocations.

Check your understanding

How many distinct patterns fit in 12 bits?

Reveal the explanation

2^12 = 4,096 patterns. This says nothing about their meaning until an encoding is chosen.

An operating model for bits, bytes & how computers work

Every apparent software abstraction eventually becomes a memory layout and a sequence of instructions. A model checkpoint is bytes on storage; loading it establishes tensors in memory; inference schedules arithmetic; a response becomes network bytes. This path explains why loading, serialization, and copying can be more important than FLOPS for small workloads.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: loading a model is a data-movement problem

Consider a 7-billion-parameter model stored in a two-byte format. The weights alone occupy roughly 14 billion bytes before file metadata, alignment, runtime allocations, or a key-value cache. Opening the file does not make it runnable: storage reads move bytes into main memory; the framework interprets those bytes as tensors; a GPU runtime may then copy or map them into device memory; only then can arithmetic begin. The slowest stage is often not multiplication. A local machine with a fast GPU can still feel slow because the checkpoint is on a slow external drive, because memory pressure forces paging, or because the model is copied twice by an accidental dtype conversion.

That path also explains why an apparent “out of memory” error is a structural diagnosis. Ask which allocation is live at the failure: immutable weights, a growing KV cache, temporary activations, a duplicate host copy, or an allocator reservation. Lowering batch size may hide the symptom, but it does not identify the owner of the bytes. The useful habit is to make a ledger before changing hardware: count elements, choose a dtype, multiply by bytes per element, then name the location and lifetime of each allocation.

Notebook: Trace a byte budget

For any performance or capacity claim, name the representation, bytes per element, working-set size, storage location, and transfer path. Those five facts prevent most unit mistakes.

items = 1_000_000
bytes_per_item = 4
working_set = items * bytes_per_item
print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB")
# Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer.
What to test next. 1. Encode: Represent a value as bits and a datatype. 2. Move: Fetch it through storage, RAM, cache, and registers. 3. Execute: Apply instructions using CPU or accelerator units. 4. Persist: Write results with an explicit format and lifetime.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Encode. Represent a value as bits and a datatype.
  2. Move. Fetch it through storage, RAM, cache, and registers.
  3. Execute. Apply instructions using CPU or accelerator units.
  4. Persist. Write results with an explicit format and lifetime.

For any performance or capacity claim, name the representation, bytes per element, working-set size, storage location, and transfer path. Those five facts prevent most unit mistakes.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

One bit pattern, several meanings

A bit pattern has no intrinsic type. The consuming instruction decides whether it represents an unsigned integer, two's-complement integer, floating-point value, text, address, or flags.

  • Unsigned integers spend every pattern on magnitude. An n-bit value covers 0 through 2ⁿ−1 and usually wraps modulo 2ⁿ.
  • IEEE 754 trades uniform spacing for dynamic range. Sign, exponent, and significand encode ordinary values plus NaN, infinities, signed zero, and subnormals.
  • UTF-8 encodes Unicode code points as bytes. A visible grapheme may contain several code points, so byte length and character count differ.

The gotcha. Reinterpreting bytes changes meaning without converting value.

Memory is a hierarchy

Registers, caches, RAM, and storage trade capacity against latency and bandwidth. Dense scans exploit locality; pointer chasing and random page access often do not.

  • Caches move lines. Reading one field fetches nearby bytes, and unrelated writes on one line can create false sharing.
  • Virtual memory translates and protects addresses. Page tables and translation caches add another locality boundary.
  • Capacity includes live intermediates. Parameters coexist with activations, gradients, optimizer state, workspaces, padding, and copies.

The gotcha. A parameter file can fit while the running model fails at its memory peak.

Instructions expose physical cost

Compilers lower source into an instruction set. Pipelines overlap stages, out-of-order execution finds independent work, vector units operate on lanes, and atomic operations coordinate selected shared updates.

  • Dependencies set the parallel ceiling. More cores cannot accelerate a serial chain.
  • Memory ordering belongs to correctness. An atomic counter does not protect a multi-step invariant.
  • Formats preserve meaning across machines. Endianness, sizes, schema versions, units, and checksums need explicit contracts.

The gotcha. Successful parsing proves structure, not semantic compatibility.
